lesson.title: 1890: The Frontier Disappears from the Map
lesson.summary: In the same year as the Wounded Knee Massacre, the U.S. Census Bureau announced it could no longer draw a line marking the edge of American settlement, a bureaucratic footnote that a young historian turned into one of the most influential ideas in American history.
lesson.body:
The ideology of Manifest Destiny, the decades long belief that had driven American settlement across the continent, was essentially declared fulfilled in 1890. In its report on that year's census, the Census Bureau noted that unsettled areas of the country had been so broken up by isolated pockets of settlement that it was no longer possible to describe a continuous "frontier line," the boundary that had traditionally divided settled territory from unsettled land on official government maps.

Three years later, in 1893, a young historian named Frederick Jackson Turner presented a paper titled "The Significance of the Frontier in American History" to the American Historical Association, meeting in Chicago alongside the World's Columbian Exposition. Turner argued that the existence of an open frontier, rather than European institutions carried across the Atlantic, had been the central force shaping American character, that the nation's democracy, individualism, and inventiveness had all grown out of the repeated experience of settling new land. With the frontier now officially closed, Turner warned, the country faced an uncertain future without the outlet for growth and renewal the frontier had supposedly provided. Turner's thesis proved enormously influential among later historians, though subsequent scholars have rightly criticized it for largely erasing Native peoples and other communities who already lived on the land Turner described as open or unsettled.

The census announcement and Turner's thesis did not emerge from nowhere. The final years of frontier expansion depended directly on policies like the Dawes Act, covered in an earlier chapter, which broke up tribal landholdings and released millions of acres of formerly Native land, including in Indian Territory in present day Oklahoma, for white settlement, most dramatically in land runs such as the 1889 opening of the Unassigned Lands, when tens of thousands of settlers raced to claim homesteads in a single day. That the census declared the frontier closed in the very same year that the Wounded Knee Massacre effectively ended armed Native resistance on the Plains was no coincidence: both events marked the final stages of the same decades long process of conquest and dispossession.

The sense that domestic expansion had reached its natural limit fed directly into new political currents of the 1890s, including growing calls for American expansion overseas, and it left a lasting mark on how Americans understood their own history: a story of opportunity and self reliance that, as this chapter and the ones before it make clear, was built on the removal and dispossession of the nations who already called that land home.
